options: The training data it threw away
One number for how wrong its answers are: 0 is perfect, and bigger is worse
How much money training cost
The number of weights it has
questions.explanation: The loss compares the model's answers with the right ones and boils it down to one number. Training is all about making that number smaller.

questions.prompt: A sentence is split into 12 tokens. How many next-token practice questions does it give an LLM?
questions.explanation: Every token after the first is the right answer to "what comes next?" given the tokens before it, so 12 tokens give 11 questions. "Mumbai gets heavy rain every monsoon." is 9 tokens and gives 8.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't an LLM need people to write the answers for its training text?
options: The text supplies its own answers: each next token is the right answer
It copies the answers from a search engine
It doesn't use answers at all
Other chatbots write the answers for it
questions.explanation: This is self-supervised learning. Our handwriting network needed a person to label every image, but in text, whatever comes next is already the answer.

questions.prompt: The right next token is "chai". Model A gave "chai" a 90% chance and model B gave it 10%. Which has the lower cross-entropy loss?
options: Model B, because it's less sure of itself
Both are the same, because they both included "chai"
Model A, because it gave the right answer a much higher chance
Neither: cross-entropy only counts wrong answers
questions.explanation: Cross-entropy looks at the chance given to the right answer: 90% gives a loss of about 0.11, while 10% gives about 2.30. The less likely a model thought the right answer was, the bigger its loss.

questions.prompt: In gradient descent, what does the gradient tell the model?
options: Which way the loss goes up, and how steeply, so it can step the other way
The right answer to every training example
How many passes are left
Which examples to delete
questions.explanation: The gradient is the slope of the loss. Each step moves the weights the opposite way, downhill, like feeling the slope under your feet in fog.

questions.prompt: While training, the loss jumps up and down and gets worse with every step. What's the most likely fix?
options: Add more layers to the network
Train for more passes
Use fewer training examples
Lower the learning rate, so each step is smaller
questions.explanation: A learning rate that's too big makes each step overshoot the valley, like the samosa example at 0.11, whose guesses swung from ₹26.45 to ₹1.89 and further out. Smaller steps let it settle.

options: It checks the training data for mistakes
It runs the network backwards to write text
It works out, for every weight, which way to nudge it, starting from the loss and working back through the layers
It removes the weights the model doesn't need
questions.explanation: With thousands or billions of weights, the model needs the gradient for each one. Backpropagation finds them all in one go, from the loss backwards. It was made famous by a 1986 paper.

questions.prompt: A model gets 100% of its practice examples right but only 60% of new ones. What's going on?
options: It's working perfectly
It's overfitting: it has mugged up its practice examples instead of learning the general pattern
Its learning rate is exactly right
The new examples must all be wrong
questions.explanation: Our network did exactly this when trained on only 30 images: 100% on those, 62.4% on new ones. More, and more varied, examples help, and testing on unseen examples is how you catch it.
